evergreen_concepts: Unit Economics: CAC vs LTV

A business is only as healthy as the gap between what it costs to acquire a customer (CAC) and the gross profit that customer returns over their life (LTV). The usual benchmark is LTV:CAC above 3:1 with payback inside 12 months; below that, growth consumes cash faster than it creates value.
Moats: Where Durable Profit Comes From

Sustainable margin comes from four things only: switching costs, network effects, scale economies, or a brand people pay extra for. If you cannot name which one protects your profit, you are renting customers from the market rather than owning them.
Porter's Five Forces
Industry profitability is set by five pressures: supplier power, buyer power, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, and rivalry. Work through them before blaming execution for thin margins.
Opportunity Cost Is the Real Price
Every yes is a no to something else. The right comparison for any decision is not 'does this help?' but 'is this the best use of the same capital, time, and attention?'
Goodhart's Law
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Metrics decay the moment incentives attach to them, so pair every KPI with a qualitative check that can catch the gaming.
Circle of Competence
Returns come from knowing the boundary of what you actually understand and staying near the edge of it. Most large losses happen while operating outside it, believing you are inside.
Second-Order Thinking
'And then what?' First-order thinking stops at the immediate effect. Durable advantage comes from anticipating how competitors, customers, and regulators will respond to your own move.
The Flywheel vs the Doom Loop

Growth compounds when each turn of the loop makes the next turn cheaper: more users, better product, lower acquisition cost. If each turn costs more, that is not a flywheel, it is a doom loop wearing one.
Skin in the Game
Advice is cheap when the advisor bears none of the downside. Weight opinions by what the speaker loses if they are wrong, and structure deals so incentives point the same way as outcomes.
Barbell Strategy
Put the large majority of resources in extremely safe positions and a small slice in very high-upside bets, while avoiding the comfortable middle where a single shock can wipe you out.
Cost Structure Beats Price
In commoditised markets the low-cost producer sets the price and survives the downturn. Ask whether your advantage is structural cost, distribution, or brand; price alone is never a strategy.
Optionality: Pay Small to Keep Choices Open
A little money or time spent preserving future choices is often worth more than the expected value of a committed path, because it lets you act when the information improves.
